title: Half of Americans Now View India Unfavorably, Pew Survey Finds
excerpt: India's favorability in the United States has dropped to its lowest point since Pew began tracking the question in 2008, with younger Americans and Republicans driving the decline.
body:
• Fifty percent of Americans now view India unfavorably, while 45% hold a favorable opinion — the most negative reading since Pew Research Center began asking the question in 2008.
  • The decline is sharpest among younger Americans: 56% of those aged 18-29 view India unfavorably, compared with 43% of those 65 and older.
  • Republicans are more negative than Democrats, with 55% of GOP-leaning respondents holding an unfavorable view compared with 47% of Democrats.
  • Globally, India's image is mixed: a median of 45% across 36 countries view India favorably, while 41% view it unfavorably.

For the first time since tracking began nearly two decades ago, a majority of Americans hold an unfavorable view of India, according to a Pew Research Center survey published this month that reveals a steady erosion of goodwill toward the world's most populous democracy.

The survey, conducted from February 9 to May 13 across 36 countries with more than 42,000 respondents, found that 50% of U.S. adults now view India unfavorably, while 45% hold a favorable opinion. The numbers represent a significant shift from 2023, when 51% of Americans viewed India favorably.

A Decline Driven by Age and Politics

The unfavorable sentiment is not distributed evenly across American society. The generational divide is striking: 56% of Americans aged 18 to 29 view India unfavorably, as do 54% of those aged 30 to 49. Among older Americans, the picture is reversed — half of those aged 50 to 64 and half of those 65 and older maintain a favorable view.

Political affiliation further shapes perceptions. Among Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, 55% hold an unfavorable view of India, compared with 42% who see the country favorably. Democrats are more evenly split, with 50% favorable and 47% unfavorable.

"Americans' opinions of India lean more unfavorable than favorable."

— Pew Research Center, Spring 2026 Global Attitudes Survey

The ideological breakdown reinforces the partisan pattern. Among self-identified liberals, 54% view India positively, compared with just 40% of conservatives.

A Sliding Trajectory

The current numbers cap a volatile few years in American perceptions of India. Favorable views stood at 51% in 2023, dropped to 43% in 2024, recovered partially to 49% in 2025, and have now fallen again to 45%. The four-point decline from 2025 to 2026 is statistically significant, Pew noted.

The timing coincides with a period of heightened friction in the U.S.-India relationship, including trade tensions, tariff disputes, and diplomatic disagreements. A separate Pew finding showed that favorable views of the United States among Indians have also declined, falling from 54% in 2025 to 45% in 2026.

India's Global Image: A Mixed Picture

Beyond the United States, India's global standing presents a complex mosaic. Across all 36 countries surveyed, a median of 45% hold a favorable view of India, while 41% view it unfavorably.

India's strongest supporters are in Sri Lanka, where 79% view the country favorably, followed by the United Kingdom and Kenya at 71% each. Germany (63%), Israel (60%), and Italy (56%) also lean positive. At the other end, Pakistan registers just 7% favorability, with Turkey at 15% and the West Bank and East Jerusalem at 18%.

Several countries have shown notable shifts since 2025. Bangladesh recorded the steepest decline, with favorable views dropping 15 percentage points to 42%. Turkey and Nigeria each fell 10 points. In contrast, the U.K. saw an 11-point increase in favorable views to 71%, and Germany rose 6 points to 63%.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the nearly 4.8 million Indian Americans living in the United States, the findings carry particular resonance. The decline in India's favorability coincides with a broader hardening of American attitudes toward immigration and foreign nations, dynamics that Indian Americans navigate in their daily lives.

The partisan divide also carries implications. Indian Americans have historically leaned Democratic, and the finding that Democrats hold a more favorable view of India than Republicans aligns with existing political patterns within the community.

The Pew survey also found that most Americans (54%) believe India's influence in the world has stayed about the same in recent years, while 30% say it is getting stronger and 13% say it has weakened.

The results underscore a reality that Indian diplomats and diaspora organizations have long grappled with: India's global image is not a settled question but a moving target shaped by geopolitics, trade policy, and the shifting currents of domestic politics in countries around the world.
